'''John Parascandola''' (born '''John Louis Parascandola''', July 14, 1941 – November 30, 2024) was an American [[History of medicine|medical historian]].  He wrote numerous books, including ''The Development of American Pharmacology: John J. Abel and the Shaping of a Discipline'', and held the position of Public Health Service Historian.<ref name="JHistMed49">{{cite journal|year=1994|journal=Journal of the History of Medicine and Allied Sciences|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|volume=49|issue=3|pages=433|issn=0022-5045 |doi=10.1093/jhmas/49.3.432|title=Awards, Fellowships, and Prizes}}</ref>

==Education==
Parascandola received his Bachelor's Degree in Chemistry from [[Brooklyn College]]<ref name="ACSbio" /> before receiving his Master's Degree in Biochemistry and his PhD in the History of Science in 1968 at the [[University of Wisconsin - Madison]].<ref name="ACSbio" />  Parascandola did post-doctoral work at [[Harvard University]].<ref name="JHistMed49" />

==Career==
Parascandola's career began in 1974 as Director of the American Institute of the History of Pharmacy, where he remained until 1981.  In 1983, Parascandola became Chief of the History of Medicine Division of the [[United States National Library of Medicine]].  In 1992, he became Public Health Service Historian, which he held until his retirement in 2004. He taught at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] and taught at the [[University of Maryland]]. He taught classes on topics such as [[Mummies]] and [[Mad Doctors in Film and Literature]] until his death in 2024.<ref name="AIHP">{{cite web|url=https://aihp.org/remembering-john-parascandola/ |title= Remembering John Parascandola |accessdate=2025-08-30}}</ref><ref name=Parascandola>{{cite web

==Writings==
Parascandola's two most recognized books were ''The Development of American Pharmacology: John J. Abel and the Shaping of a Discipline'', which was written in 1992 and received the 1994 George Urdang Medal,<ref name="JHistMed49" />  and ''Sex, Sin, and Science: A History of Syphilis in America'', which was released in 2008 and won the George Pendleton Prize for 2009.<ref name="AAHM">{{cite web|url=http://www.histmed.org/newsletters/feb2009web.pdf|title=News letter. February 2009|date=February 2009|publisher=American Association for the History of Medicine|pages=11|accessdate=2009-08-03}}</ref>

==Awards==
Parascandola was the recipient of several awards, including the [[Surgeon General of the United States|Surgeon General]]’s Exemplary Service Award, the Assistant Secretary for Health’s Superior Service Award, the [[National Institute of Health]] Merit Award, and the [[Surgeon General's Medallion]].<ref name="ACSbio">{{cite web|url=http://www.scs.uiuc.edu/~mainzv/HIST/awards/Edelstein%20Papers/BioParascandola.pdf|title=John Parascandola|last=Perfetti|first=T.A.|date=2004-12-12|publisher=[[American Chemical Society]]|accessdate=2009-07-27}}</ref> In 2002, he received the [[Sidney M. Edelstein Award for Outstanding Achievement in the History of Chemistry]] from the [[American Chemical Society]].<ref name="Edelstein">{{cite web |title=EDELSTEIN AWARD FOR OUTSTANDING ACHIEVEMENT IN THE HISTORY OF CHEMISTRY |url=http://acshist.scs.illinois.edu/awards/edelstein.php |website=American Chemical Society Division of the History of Chemistry |accessdate=22 July 2019}}</ref>

==Death==
Parascandola suffered from recurring [[lymphoma]]. He succumbed to the cause in his home in Bethesda, Maryland,  on November 30, 2024, aged 83.<ref name="AIHP">{{cite web|url=https://aihp.org/remembering-john-parascandola/ |title= Remembering John Parascandola |accessdate=2025-08-30}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.interfaithfunerals.com/obituaries/john-parascandola |title= John Louis Parascandola Obituary November 30, 2024 |accessdate=2025-08-30}}</ref>
